e-452.knowledge_point: Integrating an Expression Involving a Power Function Multiplied by Its Derivative
e-452.worked_solution:
We note that $6x^2$ is the derivative of the quantity in the parentheses. So we make a substitution

$$
u=2x^3+3.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =6{x}^{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}u=6{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and rewriting our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 6{x}^{2}(2{x}^{3}+3)^{6}\,\text{d}x & =\int (2{x}^{3}+3)^{6}\,6{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {u}^{6}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now solve the integral using the power rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{6}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{{u}^{7}}{7}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we substitute $u=2x^3+3$ back in the expression. So the final result is

$$
\displaystyle\int 6x^2(2x^3+3)^6\,\textrm{d}x =\dfrac{(2x^3+3)^7}{7}+C.
$$

e-453.knowledge_point: Integrating an Expression Involving a Power Function Multiplied by a Constant Multiple of Its Derivative
e-453.worked_solution:
The $x$ that's outside the parentheses isn't quite the derivative of $(1+2x^2).$ The derivative of $(1+2x^2)$ is $4x,$ so we're out by a constant factor of $4$. However, since we're out only by a constant factor, substitution will still work!

So we make the substitution

$$
u=1+2x^2.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =4x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x{(1+2{x}^{2})}^{6}\,\text{d}x & =\int {(1+2{x}^{2})}^{6}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {u}^{6}\cdot \frac{1}{4}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int {u}^{6}\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}\int {u}^{6}\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{{u}^{7}}{7}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{28}{u}^{7}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{28}{(1+2{x}^{2})}^{7}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

e-454.knowledge_point: Integrating a Rational Function Using Natural Logarithms
e-454.worked_solution:
Let $u=x^3+1.$ Then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = 3x^2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 1 3 \textrm d u= x^2 \, \textrm d x,
$$

and we can solve the resulting integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{3}+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{x}^{3}+1}\cdot {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|{x}^{3}+1|+C\end{aligned}
$$

e-6149.worked_solution:
Let $u = 1 - x^3.$ Then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = -3x^2 \quad \Longrightarrow\quad -\dfrac{1}{3} \textrm d u= x^2 \, \textrm d x,
$$

and we can solve the resulting integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{2}}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{3}}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{3}}}\cdot {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}\cdot (-\frac{1}{3})\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}(2\sqrt{u})+C \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{u}+C \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{1-{x}^{3}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Let u=5x^2-4, so du=10x dx. The integral becomes ∫u^(1/2) du=(2/3)u^(3/2)+C. Substituting back gives option e.

after.name: Question 1
after.worked_solution:
We note that $10x$ is the derivative of the quantity in the square root. So we make a substitution

$$
u=5{x}^{2}-4.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =10x\,⟹\,\text{d}u=10x\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and rewriting our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 10x\sqrt{5{x}^{2}-4}\,\text{d}x & =\int \sqrt{5{x}^{2}-4}\,10x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now solve the integral using the power rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{{u}^{3/2}}{(\frac{3}{2})}+C \\  & =\frac{2{u}^{3/2}}{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we substitute $u=5{x}^{2}-4$ back in the expression. So the final result is

$$
\int 10x\sqrt{5{x}^{2}-4}\,\text{d}x=\frac{2(5{x}^{2}-4)^{3/2}}{3}+C.
$$

Question 1
?

Calculate ∫10x5x2−4dx.

a
−2(5x2−4)3/23+C
b
3(5x2−4)2/3+C
c
−3(5x2−4)3/22+C
d
3(5x2−4)2/32+C
e
2(5x2−4)3/23+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We note that 10x is the derivative of the quantity in the square root. So we make a substitution u=5x2−4. Its derivative is given by

dudx=10x⟹du=10xdx,

and rewriting our integral, we get ∫10x5x2−4dx=∫5x2−410xdx=∫udu=∫u1/2du.

We can now solve the integral using the power rule: ∫u1/2du=u3/2(32)+C=2u3/23+C

Lastly, we substitute u=5x2−4 back in the expression. So the final result is ∫10x5x2−4dx=2(5x2−4)3/23+C.

content.knowledge_point: Integrating an Expression Involving a Power Function Multiplied by Its Derivative
content.worked_solution:
We note that $10x$ is the derivative of the quantity in the square root. So we make a substitution

$$
u=5{x}^{2}-4.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =10x\,⟹\,\text{d}u=10x\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and rewriting our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 10x\sqrt{5{x}^{2}-4}\,\text{d}x & =\int \sqrt{5{x}^{2}-4}\,10x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now solve the integral using the power rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{{u}^{3/2}}{(\frac{3}{2})}+C \\  & =\frac{2{u}^{3/2}}{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we substitute $u=5{x}^{2}-4$ back in the expression. So the final result is

$$
\int 10x\sqrt{5{x}^{2}-4}\,\text{d}x=\frac{2(5{x}^{2}-4)^{3/2}}{3}+C.
$$

after.name: Question 2
after.worked_solution:
We note that $5{x}^{4}$ is the derivative of the quantity in the radical. So we make a substitution

$$
u=1+{x}^{5}.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =5{x}^{4}\,⟹\,\text{d}u=5{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and rewriting our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{5{x}^{4}}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{5}}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{5}}}\,5{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int \frac{1}{{u}^{1/2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int {u}^{-1/2}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now solve the integral using the power rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{-1/2}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{{u}^{1/2}}{(\frac{1}{2})}+C \\  & =2{u}^{1/2}+C \\  & =2\sqrt{u}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we substitute $u=1+{x}^{5}$ back in the expression. So the final result is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{5{x}^{4}}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{5}}}\,\text{d}x & =2\sqrt{1+{x}^{5}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}\int \frac{5{x}^{4}}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{5}}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{5}}}\,5{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int \frac{1}{{u}^{1/2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int {u}^{-1/2}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now solve the integral using the power rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{-1/2}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{{u}^{1/2}}{(\frac{1}{2})}+C \\  & =2{u}^{1/2}+C \\  & =2\sqrt{u}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we substitute $u=1+{x}^{5}$ back in the expression. So the final result is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{5{x}^{4}}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{5}}}\,\text{d}x & =2\sqrt{1+{x}^{5}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate ∫3x2(x3+4)5dx.

a
(x3+4)55+C
b
3x2(x3+4)62+C
c
(x3+4)66x+C

decision.explanation: Let u=x^3+4, so du=3x^2 dx. Then ∫u^5 du=u^6/6+C. Substituting back gives (x^3+4)^6/6+C, matching option d.

after.name: Question 3
after.worked_solution:
We note that $3{x}^{2}$ is the derivative of the quantity in the parentheses. So we make a substitution

$$
u={x}^{3}+4.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =3{x}^{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}u=3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and rewriting our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3{x}^{2}({x}^{3}+4)^{5}\,\text{d}x & =\int ({x}^{3}+4)^{5}\,3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {u}^{5}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now solve the integral using the power rule:

$$
\int {u}^{5}\,\text{d}u=\frac{{u}^{6}}{6}+C
$$

Lastly, we substitute $u={x}^{3}+4$ back in the expression. So the final result is

$$
\int 3{x}^{2}({x}^{3}+4)^{5}\,\text{d}x=\frac{({x}^{3}+4)^{6}}{6}+C.
$$

after.html:
Question 3
?

Calculate ∫3x2(x3+4)5dx.

a
(x3+4)55+C
b
3x2(x3+4)62+C
c
(x3+4)66x+C
d
(x3+4)66+C
e
3x(x3+4)62+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We note that 3x2 is the derivative of the quantity in the parentheses. So we make a substitution u=x3+4. Its derivative is given by

dudx=3x2⟹du=3x2dx,

and rewriting our integral, we get ∫3x2(x3+4)5dx=∫(x3+4)53x2dx=∫u5du.

We can now solve the integral using the power rule: ∫u5du=u66+C

Lastly, we substitute u=x3+4 back in the expression. So the final result is ∫3x2(x3+4)5dx=(x3+4)66+C.

content.knowledge_point: Integrating an Expression Involving a Power Function Multiplied by Its Derivative
content.worked_solution:
We note that $3{x}^{2}$ is the derivative of the quantity in the parentheses. So we make a substitution

$$
u={x}^{3}+4.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =3{x}^{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}u=3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and rewriting our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3{x}^{2}({x}^{3}+4)^{5}\,\text{d}x & =\int ({x}^{3}+4)^{5}\,3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {u}^{5}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now solve the integral using the power rule:

$$
\int {u}^{5}\,\text{d}u=\frac{{u}^{6}}{6}+C
$$

Lastly, we substitute $u={x}^{3}+4$ back in the expression. So the final result is

$$
\int 3{x}^{2}({x}^{3}+4)^{5}\,\text{d}x=\frac{({x}^{3}+4)^{6}}{6}+C.
$$

after.name: Question 4
after.worked_solution:
We note that $2x$ is the derivative of the quantity in the parentheses. So we make a substitution

$$
u={x}^{2}+1.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =2x\,⟹\,\text{d}u=2x\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and rewriting our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2x({x}^{2}+1)^{12}\,\text{d}x & =\int ({x}^{2}+1)^{12}\,2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {u}^{12}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now solve the integral using the power rule:

$$
\int {u}^{12}\,\text{d}u=\frac{{u}^{13}}{13}+C
$$

Lastly, we substitute $u={x}^{2}+1$ back in the expression. So the final result is

$$
\int 2x({x}^{2}+1)^{12}\,\text{d}x=\frac{({x}^{2}+1)^{13}}{13}+C.
$$

Calculate ∫12x52x6−3dx.

a
2(2x6−3)3/23+C
b

decision.explanation: Let u=2x^6-3, so du=12x^5 dx. Then ∫u^(1/2) du=(2/3)u^(3/2)+C. Substituting back gives option a.

after.name: Question 5
after.worked_solution:
We note that $12{x}^{5}$ is the derivative of the quantity in the square root. So we make a substitution

$$
u=2{x}^{6}-3.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =12{x}^{5}\,⟹\,\text{d}u=12{x}^{5}\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and rewriting our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 12{x}^{5}\sqrt{2{x}^{6}-3}\,\text{d}x & =\int \sqrt{2{x}^{6}-3}\cdot 12{x}^{5}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now solve the integral using the power rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{{u}^{3/2}}{(\frac{3}{2})}+C \\  & =\frac{2{u}^{3/2}}{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we substitute $u=2{x}^{6}-3$ back in the expression. So the final result is

$$
\int 12{x}^{5}\sqrt{2{x}^{6}-3}\,\text{d}x=\frac{2(2{x}^{6}-3)^{3/2}}{3}+C.
$$

Question 5
?

Calculate ∫12x52x6−3dx.

a
2(2x6−3)3/23+C
b
−122x6−3+C
c
−22x6−3+C
d
3(2x6−3)3/22+C
e
(2x6−3)3/22+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We note that 12x5 is the derivative of the quantity in the square root. So we make a substitution u=2x6−3. Its derivative is given by

dudx=12x5⟹du=12x5dx,

and rewriting our integral, we get ∫12x52x6−3dx=∫2x6−3⋅12x5dx=∫udu=∫u1/2du.

We can now solve the integral using the power rule: ∫u1/2du=u3/2(32)+C=2u3/23+C

Lastly, we substitute u=2x6−3 back in the expression. So the final result is ∫12x52x6−3dx=2(2x6−3)3/23+C.

content.knowledge_point: Integrating an Expression Involving a Power Function Multiplied by Its Derivative
content.worked_solution:
We note that $12{x}^{5}$ is the derivative of the quantity in the square root. So we make a substitution

$$
u=2{x}^{6}-3.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =12{x}^{5}\,⟹\,\text{d}u=12{x}^{5}\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and rewriting our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 12{x}^{5}\sqrt{2{x}^{6}-3}\,\text{d}x & =\int \sqrt{2{x}^{6}-3}\cdot 12{x}^{5}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now solve the integral using the power rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{{u}^{3/2}}{(\frac{3}{2})}+C \\  & =\frac{2{u}^{3/2}}{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we substitute $u=2{x}^{6}-3$ back in the expression. So the final result is

$$
\int 12{x}^{5}\sqrt{2{x}^{6}-3}\,\text{d}x=\frac{2(2{x}^{6}-3)^{3/2}}{3}+C.
$$

decision.explanation: Let u=x^2-1, so du=2x dx and x dx=du/2. Thus the integral is (1/2)∫u^3 du=u^4/8+C, giving option c.

after.name: Question 6
after.worked_solution:
In this case, the $x$ that's outside the parentheses isn't quite the derivative of $({x}^{2}-1).$ But the derivative is $2x,$ so we're only out by a constant factor.
So we make the substitution

$$
u={x}^{2}-1.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =2x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x({x}^{2}-1)^{3}\,\text{d}x & =\int ({x}^{2}-1)^{3}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {u}^{3}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int {u}^{3}\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\int {u}^{3}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{{u}^{4}}{4}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{u}^{4}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{8}({x}^{2}-1)^{4}+C \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}-1)^{4}}{8}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6
?

Calculate ∫x(x2−1)3dx.

a
8(x2−1)4+C
b
3(x2−1)3+C
c
(x2−1)48+C
d
(x2−1)510+C
e
(x2−1)36+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

In this case, the x that's outside the parentheses isn't quite the derivative of (x2−1). But the derivative is 2x, so we're only out by a constant factor. So we make the substitution u=x2−1. Its derivative is given by

dudx=2x⟹12du=xdx,

and we can now write our integral in terms of u, as follows:

∫x(x2−1)3dx=∫(x2−1)3⋅xdx=∫u3⋅12du=12∫u3du

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of u and then write the final result in terms of x. We get

12∫u3du=12⋅u44+C=18u4+C=18(x2−1)4+C=(x2−1)48+C.

content.knowledge_point: Integrating an Expression Involving a Power Function Multiplied by a Constant Multiple of Its Derivative
content.worked_solution:
In this case, the $x$ that's outside the parentheses isn't quite the derivative of $({x}^{2}-1).$ But the derivative is $2x,$ so we're only out by a constant factor.
So we make the substitution

$$
u={x}^{2}-1.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =2x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x({x}^{2}-1)^{3}\,\text{d}x & =\int ({x}^{2}-1)^{3}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {u}^{3}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int {u}^{3}\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\int {u}^{3}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{{u}^{4}}{4}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{u}^{4}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{8}({x}^{2}-1)^{4}+C \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}-1)^{4}}{8}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Let u=x^2-5, so x dx=du/2. Then the integral is (1/2)∫u^(1/2) du=(1/3)u^(3/2)+C, matching option a.

after.name: Question 7
after.worked_solution:
In this case, the $x$ that's outside the square root isn't quite the derivative of $({x}^{2}-5).$ But the derivative is $2x,$ so we're only out by a constant factor.

So we make the substitution

$$
u={x}^{2}-5.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =2x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x\sqrt{{x}^{2}-5}\,\text{d}x & =\int \sqrt{{x}^{2}-5}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{{u}^{3/2}}{(\frac{3}{2})}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{2}{3}\cdot {u}^{3/2}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{u}^{3/2}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{{u}^{3}}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{({x}^{2}-5)^{3}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

In this case, the x that's outside the square root isn't quite the derivative of (x2−5). But the derivative is 2x, so we're only out by a constant factor.

So we make the substitution u=x2−5. Its derivative is given by

dudx=2x⟹12du=xdx,

and we can now write our integral in terms of u, as follows:

∫xx2−5dx=∫x2−5⋅xdx=∫u⋅12du=12∫u1/2du

content.knowledge_point: Integrating an Expression Involving a Power Function Multiplied by a Constant Multiple of Its Derivative
content.worked_solution:
In this case, the $x$ that's outside the square root isn't quite the derivative of $({x}^{2}-5).$ But the derivative is $2x,$ so we're only out by a constant factor.

So we make the substitution

$$
u={x}^{2}-5.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =2x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x\sqrt{{x}^{2}-5}\,\text{d}x & =\int \sqrt{{x}^{2}-5}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{{u}^{3/2}}{(\frac{3}{2})}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{2}{3}\cdot {u}^{3/2}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{u}^{3/2}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{{u}^{3}}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{({x}^{2}-5)^{3}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 8
after.worked_solution:
In this case, the $2{x}^{7}$ that's outside the parentheses isn't quite the derivative of $(1+{x}^{8}).$ But the derivative is $8{x}^{7},$ so we're only out by a constant factor. 

So we make the substitution

$$
u=1+{x}^{8}.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =8{x}^{7}\,⟹\,\frac{1}{8}\text{d}u={x}^{7}\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2{x}^{7}{(1+{x}^{8})}^{7}\,\text{d}x & =\int 2{(1+{x}^{8})}^{7}\cdot {x}^{7}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int 2{u}^{7}\cdot \frac{1}{8}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int {u}^{7}\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}\int {u}^{7}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{{u}^{8}}{8}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{32}{u}^{8}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{32}{(1+{x}^{8})}^{8}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

after.html:
Question 8
?

∫2x7(1+x8)7dx=

a
132(1+x8)8+C
b
7(1+x8)7+C
c
18(1+x8)8+C
d
8(1+x8)8+C
e
156(1+x8)7+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

In this case, the 2x7 that's outside the parentheses isn't quite the derivative of (1+x8). But the derivative is 8x7, so we're only out by a constant factor.

So we make the substitution u=1+x8. Its derivative is given by

dudx=8x7⟹18du=x7dx,

and we can now write our integral in terms of u, as follows:

∫2x7(1+x8)7dx=∫2(1+x8)7⋅x7dx=∫2u7⋅18du=14∫u7du

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of u and then write the final result in terms of x. We get

14∫u7du=14⋅u88+C=132u8+C=132(1+x8)8+C.

content.knowledge_point: Integrating an Expression Involving a Power Function Multiplied by a Constant Multiple of Its Derivative
content.worked_solution:
In this case, the $2{x}^{7}$ that's outside the parentheses isn't quite the derivative of $(1+{x}^{8}).$ But the derivative is $8{x}^{7},$ so we're only out by a constant factor. 

So we make the substitution

$$
u=1+{x}^{8}.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =8{x}^{7}\,⟹\,\frac{1}{8}\text{d}u={x}^{7}\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2{x}^{7}{(1+{x}^{8})}^{7}\,\text{d}x & =\int 2{(1+{x}^{8})}^{7}\cdot {x}^{7}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int 2{u}^{7}\cdot \frac{1}{8}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int {u}^{7}\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}\int {u}^{7}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{{u}^{8}}{8}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{32}{u}^{8}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{32}{(1+{x}^{8})}^{8}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Let u=x^4+11, so du=4x^3 dx. The integral becomes (1/4)∫u^9 du=u^10/40+C, matching option c.

after.name: Question 9
after.worked_solution:
In this case, the ${x}^{3}$ that's outside the parentheses isn't quite the derivative of $({x}^{4}+11).$ But the derivative is $4{x}^{3},$ so we're only out by a constant factor. 

So we make the substitution

$$
u={x}^{4}+11.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =4{x}^{3}\,⟹\,\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u={x}^{3}\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{3}{({x}^{4}+11)}^{9}\,\text{d}x & =\int ({x}^{4}+11)^{9}\cdot {x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {u}^{9}\cdot \frac{1}{4}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int {u}^{9}\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}\int {u}^{9}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{{u}^{10}}{10}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{40}{u}^{10}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{40}({x}^{4}+11)^{10}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 10
after.worked_solution:
In this case, the ${x}^{2}$ that's outside the parentheses isn't quite the derivative of $(2{x}^{3}+1).$ But the derivative is $6{x}^{2},$ so we're only out by a constant factor. 

So we make the substitution

$$
u=2{x}^{3}+1.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =6{x}^{2}\,⟹\,\frac{1}{6}\text{d}u={x}^{2}\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}{(2{x}^{3}+1)}^{5}\,\text{d}x & =\int (2{x}^{3}+1)^{5}\cdot {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {u}^{5}\cdot \frac{1}{6}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\int {u}^{5}\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6}\int {u}^{5}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{6}\cdot \frac{{u}^{6}}{6}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{36}{u}^{6}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{36}(2{x}^{3}+1)^{6}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

after.html:
Question 10
?

∫x2(2x3+1)5dx=

a
15(2x3+1)5+C
b
110(2x3+1)5+C
c
16(2x3+1)6+C
d
136(2x3+1)6+C
e
10(2x3+1)5+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

In this case, the x2 that's outside the parentheses isn't quite the derivative of (2x3+1). But the derivative is 6x2, so we're only out by a constant factor.

So we make the substitution u=2x3+1. Its derivative is given by

dudx=6x2⟹16du=x2dx,

and we can now write our integral in terms of u, as follows:

∫x2(2x3+1)5dx=∫(2x3+1)5⋅x2dx=∫u5⋅16du=16∫u5du

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of u and then write the final result in terms of x. We get

16∫u5du=16⋅u66+C=136u6+C=136(2x3+1)6+C.

content.knowledge_point: Integrating an Expression Involving a Power Function Multiplied by a Constant Multiple of Its Derivative
content.worked_solution:
In this case, the ${x}^{2}$ that's outside the parentheses isn't quite the derivative of $(2{x}^{3}+1).$ But the derivative is $6{x}^{2},$ so we're only out by a constant factor. 

So we make the substitution

$$
u=2{x}^{3}+1.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =6{x}^{2}\,⟹\,\frac{1}{6}\text{d}u={x}^{2}\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}{(2{x}^{3}+1)}^{5}\,\text{d}x & =\int (2{x}^{3}+1)^{5}\cdot {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {u}^{5}\cdot \frac{1}{6}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\int {u}^{5}\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6}\int {u}^{5}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{6}\cdot \frac{{u}^{6}}{6}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{36}{u}^{6}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{36}(2{x}^{3}+1)^{6}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 11
?

Calculate ∫1−4x31+x−x4dx.

a
ln⁡|1+x−x4|+C
b
ln⁡|1+x−x41−4x3|+C
c
ln⁡|1+x−x4|1−4x3+C
d
ln⁡|1−4x3|+C
e
ln⁡|1−4x31+x−x4|+C
Submit

decision.explanation: Let u=1+x-x^4, so du=(1-4x^3) dx. The integral becomes ∫du/u=ln|u|+C, matching option a.

after.name: Question 11
after.worked_solution:
Let $u=1+x-{x}^{4}.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1-4{x}^{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}u=(1-4{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x,
$$

and we can solve the resulting integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1-4{x}^{3}}{1+x-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{1+x-{x}^{4}}\cdot (1-4{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|1+x-{x}^{4}|+C\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

content.knowledge_point: Integrating a Rational Function Using Natural Logarithms
content.worked_solution:
Let $u=1+x-{x}^{4}.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1-4{x}^{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}u=(1-4{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x,
$$

and we can solve the resulting integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1-4{x}^{3}}{1+x-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{1+x-{x}^{4}}\cdot (1-4{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|1+x-{x}^{4}|+C\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 12
after.worked_solution:
Let $u={x}^{2}+1.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x,
$$

and we can solve the resulting integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{4x}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x & =4\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & =4\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)+C\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Integrating a Rational Function Using Natural Logarithms
content.worked_solution:
Let $u={x}^{2}+1.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x,
$$

and we can solve the resulting integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{4x}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x & =4\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & =4\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)+C\end{aligned}
$$

Question 13
?

Calculate ∫5x4−1x5−xdx.

a
ln⁡|x5−x|+C
b
ln⁡|5x4−1x5−x|+C
c
ln⁡|x5−x5x4−1|+C
d
ln⁡|x5−x|5x4−1+C
e
ln⁡|5x4−1|+C

decision.explanation: Let u=x^5-x, so du=(5x^4-1) dx. The integral becomes ∫du/u=ln|u|+C, matching option a.

after.name: Question 13
after.worked_solution:
Let $u={x}^{5}-x.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=5{x}^{4}-1\,⟹\,\text{d}u=(5{x}^{4}-1)\,\text{d}x,
$$

and we can solve the resulting integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{5{x}^{4}-1}{{x}^{5}-x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{x}^{5}-x}\cdot (5{x}^{4}-1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|{x}^{5}-x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

Question 13

Calculate ∫5x4−1x5−xdx.

a
ln⁡|x5−x|+C
b
ln⁡|5x4−1x5−x|+C
c
ln⁡|x5−x5x4−1|+C
d
ln⁡|x5−x|5x4−1+C
e
ln⁡|5x4−1|+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let u=x5−x. Then dudx=5x4−1⟹du=(5x4−1)dx,

and we can solve the resulting integral as follows:

∫5x4−1x5−xdx=∫1x5−x⋅(5x4−1)dx=∫1udu=ln⁡|u|+C=ln⁡|x5−x|+C

content.knowledge_point: Integrating a Rational Function Using Natural Logarithms
content.worked_solution:
Let $u={x}^{5}-x.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=5{x}^{4}-1\,⟹\,\text{d}u=(5{x}^{4}-1)\,\text{d}x,
$$

and we can solve the resulting integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{5{x}^{4}-1}{{x}^{5}-x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{x}^{5}-x}\cdot (5{x}^{4}-1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|{x}^{5}-x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Let u=2-5x^5, so du=-25x^4 dx and 10x^4 dx=-(2/5)du. Thus the integral is -(2/5)∫du/u=-(2/5)ln|2-5x^5|+C, matching option d.

after.name: Question 14
after.worked_solution:
Let $u=2-5{x}^{5}.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-25{x}^{4}\,⟹\,(-\frac{1}{25})\text{d}u={x}^{4}\,\text{d}x,
$$

and we can solve the resulting integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{10{x}^{4}}{2-5{x}^{5}}\,\text{d}x & =10\int \frac{1}{2-5{x}^{5}}\cdot {x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =10\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot (-\frac{1}{25})\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{10}{25}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{2}{5}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{2}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =-\frac{2}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡|2-5{x}^{5}|+C\end{aligned}

content.knowledge_point: Integrating a Rational Function Using Natural Logarithms
content.worked_solution:
Let $u=2-5{x}^{5}.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-25{x}^{4}\,⟹\,(-\frac{1}{25})\text{d}u={x}^{4}\,\text{d}x,
$$

and we can solve the resulting integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{10{x}^{4}}{2-5{x}^{5}}\,\text{d}x & =10\int \frac{1}{2-5{x}^{5}}\cdot {x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =10\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot (-\frac{1}{25})\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{10}{25}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{2}{5}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{2}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =-\frac{2}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡|2-5{x}^{5}|+C\end{aligned}
$$

Question 15
?

Calculate the integral of x2x3+10 with respect to x.

a
12ln⁡|x3+10|+C
b
110ln⁡|x3+10|+C
c
ln⁡|x3+10|+C
d
13ln⁡|x3+10|+C
e
3ln⁡|x3+10|+C
Submit

decision.explanation: Let u=x^3+10, so du=3x^2 dx. The integral becomes (1/3)∫du/u=(1/3)ln|x^3+10|+C, matching option d.

after.name: Question 15
after.problem: Calculate the integral of $\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{3}+10}$ with respect to $x.$
after.worked_solution:
Let $u={x}^{3}+10.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3{x}^{2}\,⟹\,\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u={x}^{2}\,\text{d}x,
$$

and we can solve the resulting integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{3}+10}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{x}^{3}+10}\cdot {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|{x}^{3}+10|+C\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Integrating a Rational Function Using Natural Logarithms
content.problem: Calculate the integral of $\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{3}+10}$ with respect to $x.$
content.worked_solution:
Let $u={x}^{3}+10.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3{x}^{2}\,⟹\,\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u={x}^{2}\,\text{d}x,
$$

and we can solve the resulting integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{3}+10}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{x}^{3}+10}\cdot {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|{x}^{3}+10|+C\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Let u=9-x^2, so x dx=-du/2. The integral is -(1/2)∫u^(-5) du=u^(-4)/8+C, matching option a.

after.name: Question 16
after.worked_solution:
Let $u=9-{x}^{2}.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2x\,⟹\,(-\frac{1}{2})\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x,
$$

and we can solve the resulting integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x}{{(9-{x}^{2})}^{5}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{(9-{x}^{2})}^{5}}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{{u}^{5}}\cdot (-\frac{1}{2})\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{{u}^{5}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{1}{4{u}^{4}})+C \\  & =\frac{1}{8{u}^{4}}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{8(9-{x}^{2})^{4}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate ∫x(9−x2)5dx.

a
18(9−x2)4+C
b

c
14(9−x2)4+C
d
(9−x2)4+C
e
12(9−x2)3+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let u=9−x2. Then

dudx=−2x⟹(−12)du=xdx,

and we can solve the resulting integral as follows:

∫x(9−x2)5dx=∫1(9−x2)5⋅xdx=∫1u5⋅(−12)du=−12∫1u5du=−12(−14u4)+C=18u4+C=18(9−x2)4+C

content.worked_solution:
Let $u=9-{x}^{2}.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2x\,⟹\,(-\frac{1}{2})\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x,
$$

and we can solve the resulting integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x}{{(9-{x}^{2})}^{5}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{(9-{x}^{2})}^{5}}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{{u}^{5}}\cdot (-\frac{1}{2})\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{{u}^{5}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{1}{4{u}^{4}})+C \\  & =\frac{1}{8{u}^{4}}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{8(9-{x}^{2})^{4}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 17
after.worked_solution:
Let $u=3-{x}^{5}.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-5{x}^{4}\,⟹\,-\frac{7}{5}\text{d}u=7{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x,
$$

and we can solve the resulting integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{7{x}^{4}}{{(3-{x}^{5})}^{6}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{(3-{x}^{5})}^{6}}\cdot 7{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{{u}^{6}}\cdot (-\frac{7}{5})\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{7}{5}\int \frac{1}{{u}^{6}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{7}{5}(-\frac{1}{5{u}^{5}})+C \\  & =\frac{7}{25{u}^{5}}+C \\  & =\frac{7}{25(3-{x}^{5})^{5}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 18
after.worked_solution:
Let $u={s}^{5}+1.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}s}=5{s}^{4}\,⟹\,\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u={s}^{4}\,\text{d}s,
$$

and we can solve the resulting integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{10{s}^{4}}{\sqrt{{s}^{5}+1}}\,\text{d}s & =10\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{s}^{5}+1}}\cdot {s}^{4}\,\text{d}s \\  & =10\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}\cdot \frac{1}{5}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{10}{5}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\cdot (2\sqrt{u})+C \\  & =4\sqrt{u}+C \\  & =4\sqrt{{s}^{5}+1}+C\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Let u=x^2+5, so x dx=du/2. The integral is (1/2)∫u^(-10) du=-u^(-9)/18+C, matching option e.

after.name: Question 19
after.worked_solution:
Let $u={x}^{2}+5.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x,
$$

and we can solve the resulting integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x}{{({x}^{2}+5)}^{10}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{({x}^{2}+5)}^{10}}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{{u}^{10}}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{{u}^{10}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{1}{9{u}^{9}})+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{18{u}^{9}}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{18({x}^{2}+5)^{9}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Question 19
?

Calculate ∫x(x2+5)10dx.

a
−19(x2+5)9+C
b
19(x2+5)9+C
c
118(x2+5)8+C
d
−12(x2+5)8+C
e
−118(x2+5)9+C
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let u=x2+5. Then dudx=2x⟹12du=xdx,

and we can solve the resulting integral as follows:

∫x(x2+5)10dx=∫1(x2+5)10⋅xdx=∫1u10⋅12du=12∫1u10du=12(−19u9)+C=−118u9+C=−118(x2+5)9+C

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option e. With u=x^2+5, x dx=du/2, giving (1/2)∫u^(-10) du=-1/(18u^9)+C. Differentiating the result gives x/(x^2+5)^10.

content.knowledge_point: Integrating Other Fractional Expressions
content.worked_solution:
Let $u={x}^{2}+5.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x,
$$

and we can solve the resulting integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x}{{({x}^{2}+5)}^{10}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{({x}^{2}+5)}^{10}}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{{u}^{10}}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{{u}^{10}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{1}{9{u}^{9}})+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{18{u}^{9}}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{18({x}^{2}+5)^{9}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 20
after.worked_solution:
Let $u=1-{y}^{4}.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}y}=-4{y}^{3}\,⟹\,(-\frac{1}{4})\text{d}u={y}^{3}\,\text{d}y,
$$

and we can solve the resulting integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{4{y}^{3}}{{(1-{y}^{4})}^{5}}\,\text{d}y & =4\int \frac{1}{{(1-{y}^{4})}^{5}}\cdot {y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =4\int \frac{1}{{u}^{5}}\cdot (-\frac{1}{4})\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{4}{4}\int \frac{1}{{u}^{5}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\int \frac{1}{{u}^{5}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-(-\frac{1}{4{u}^{4}})+C \\  & =\frac{1}{4{u}^{4}}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{4{(1-{y}^{4})}^{4}}+C\end{aligned}
$$
